problem: A well field pumps a soft confined aquifer for six months, rests for six months and repeats. The ground subsides around the wells, partly rebounds in each rest season and keeps a growing subsidence farther out.
result: Largest subsidence error at the observation wells on the 25 m mesh (peak subsidence 24.1 cm): 0.32 cm at 250 m, 0.10 cm at 500 m, 0.01 cm at 1000 m. Over 250–1500 m after the first frame, the largest subsidence error is 7.0% of the largest subsidence in the same frame, and the largest pressure error 0.4% of the largest pressure drop; at the first frame (0.12 yr, a cone only a few elements wide) the subsidence error is 12.8%.
scope: 3D quarter of a 6 km square, 50 m thick; Q = 0.02 m$^3$/s; PT (adaptive dynamic relaxation). The run in the result above uses the 25 m mesh with 416 steps; with 104 steps its well errors were 250 m: 1.41 cm, 500 m: 0.42 cm, 1000 m: 0.09 cm. Meshes at 104 steps 100, 50, 25 m: subsidence errors after the first frame 20.5%, 18.3%, 13.0%. The step dominates near each rate change: on the 50 m mesh, 416 steps give pressure 0.9% and subsidence 12.1% after the first frame (against 3.8% and 18.3%), and the worst 250 m well error falls from 1.46 to 0.41 cm. (a) bowl at the ends of the seasons; (b) observation wells; (c) errors by mesh and step: open markers 104 steps, solid 416.
meaning: This applies the verified pumping and averaged-aquifer physics at field scale, with a realistic schedule and rebound. The reference is the averaged model of a closed basin: fixed outer walls add a uniform areal strain $h(t)$ that deepens the drawdown everywhere, which the infinite-domain line well misses by up to about 20% in the rest seasons. Only changes from the initial state are computed; gravity, an overlying aquitard and inelastic compaction of clays, which set most real subsidence, are not modelled.
